description: We are a new group looking to have fun, but also aim to make Global nominee.
summary: Lunar Rocks: Beyond the Mission is an interactive website that tells the stories of the machines humanity left behind on the Moon and Mars. When a mission ends, its landers, rovers and equipment usually stay where they stopped, and most people never learn what became of them. Our site turns that history into a mission. They check in as a Space Agent, launch through a warp-jump sequence and land on the Moon. There, they explore Surveyor 3 and Apollo 11, 12 and 15, then travel to Mars to meet Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity and Perseverance. Each machine tells its story alongside real NASA facts and links to the official mission page. Back on Earth, a five-question quiz checks what visitors learned. This matters because these machines opened the way for everything we know about our nearest worlds, and they should be remembered.
details:
What it does: Lunar Rocks is a browser-based journey in six stops:

  1. Check in: visitors enter a Space Agent name, which the site uses to greet them on later pages.
  2. Launch: a countdown and warp-jump animation take them to a lunar base.
  3. The Moon: a timeline of Surveyor 3 (1967), Apollo 11 (1969), Apollo 12 (1969) and Apollo 15 (1971). It has year buttons, crewed and uncrewed tags, a counter of missions explored, and a NASA link on every card.
  4. Transit: a live rocket tracker shows the trip from the Moon to Mars.
  5. Mars: a timeline of five rovers. Each rover “speaks” in an imagined first-person story next to real mission facts. Green and orange tags show which missions are active and which have ended, and the page has a light/dark mode toggle.
  6. Return home: a five-question quiz with star ratings and instant explanations, plus a resources page that links to NASA and the NSSDCA spacecraft catalog.

Benefits and impact: Visitors learn by doing instead of reading a list of facts. The first-person stories make the hardware left behind feel memorable and human. Every fact traces back to an official NASA source. The site runs in any browser with no install, account or login, so students and the public can use it anywhere.

Tools: HTML5, CSS3 and vanilla JavaScript with no frameworks. The animated starfields use the HTML Canvas API, the agent name is stored with localStorage, and pages change with CSS view transitions. The code is managed with Git and GitHub. Images come from the NASA Image and Video Library and mission facts from NASA and NSSDCA.

Creativity: Most sites about space history read like encyclopedias. We built a story the visitor plays through, with launch sequences, landing checks and a debrief. The machines become characters instead of entries in a table.

Factors we considered: We checked the facts against NASA and labelled the first-person stories as imagined. We kept the language simple for younger audiences and used readable contrast plus a light-mode option. The animations respect the reduced-motion setting, and pages load quickly.
